rules.statement: In a PowerShell script, when an `if`, `switch` or loop statement is used as a value that must be an array, wrap the whole statement in `@(...)` rather than wrapping each branch.
rules.why: A statement used as a value unrolls its output: an empty array becomes `$null` and a single item becomes that item, so `.Count` throws under `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest`. Wrapping each branch doesn't stop this.
rules.check: Look for assignments like `$x = if (...) { ... } else { ... }` or `$x = foreach ...` whose result is later used as an array (`.Count`, indexing), where the statement isn't wrapped in `@(...)`, or only the branches are wrapped.

rules.statement: In a PowerShell script, pass an indexed or member-access value to a native command as a subexpression inside a quoted argument (`"body=$($map[$id])"`), never as `$map[$id]` or `$obj.Member` written directly in the argument.
rules.why: Native command arguments expand only a bare variable; `[...]` and `.Member` stay literal text, so the command gets the object's type name followed by the literal suffix.
rules.check: Look at calls to native executables (gh, git, dotnet, docker, etc.) for arguments containing `$var[...]` or `$var.Prop` that aren't inside `$( )`.

rules.statement: In a PowerShell script, check prerequisites such as Docker or a completed build only after the script has decided it has work to do, so a run that selects nothing reports its verdict without needing them.
rules.why: A run that selects nothing, such as an affected-only run with nothing affected, should succeed without needing Docker or a build.
rules.check: Look for prerequisite checks (tool availability, Docker running, build steps) placed before the selection logic that can decide there's nothing to do.

rules.statement: In a PowerShell fixture test, create the fixture as a temporary directory (initialized as a git repository when the script under test reads git) and delete it in a `finally` block.
rules.why: The conventions require isolated fixtures that are always cleaned up, even when the test fails.
rules.check: Look in `*.tests.ps1` files for fixtures created in the working tree or in shared locations, or temp directories that aren't removed in a `finally` block.

rules.statement: In a PowerShell test that asserts a script's `return` or `throw`, run the script in a child `pwsh -NoProfile -File` process rather than dot-sourcing or invoking it in the test's own session.
rules.why: A child process keeps the script's exit, return and thrown errors from ending or polluting the test's own session, and lets the test assert on them reliably.
rules.check: Look in `*.tests.ps1` files for scripts invoked with `&` or `.` in the same session when the test asserts on their return value or thrown error.

rules.statement: Give each build PowerShell script a fixture test named `<script>.tests.ps1` in the build scripts' tests folder, and run it as an early stage of the definition-of-done script that doesn't need a build.
rules.why: Build scripts are tested by fixtures that run before any build, so failures show up quickly.
rules.check: Look for new or changed build scripts with no matching `<script>.tests.ps1`, or a tests file that isn't wired into the early stage of the definition-of-done script.
